title: How to Find a Reliable PG in Bangalore Without Getting Scammed
metaDescription: Step-by-step guide to finding a trustworthy PG in Bangalore, spotting red flags, and securing a safe rental agreement.
intro: Moving to Bangalore for work or studies means finding a decent PG quickly — and that urgency makes you vulnerable. Fake landlords, undisclosed rules, missing amenities, and sudden evictions are real problems. This guide walks you through the process of vetting a PG properly so you don't lose money or end up in a bad living situation.

sections.heading: Start by Narrowing Your Search to Actual Neighborhoods
sections.body: Don't just search "PG in Bangalore" — you'll drown. Pick 2–3 neighborhoods that match your office or college location and your budget. Areas like Indiranagar, Koramangala, Whitefield, and Marathahalli have steady PG supply and good transport links, but they're pricier. Cheaper alternatives like Hebbal, Yeshwanthpur, or Yelahanka still have decent connectivity. Once you've picked a zone, use LocalsIndia to browse listings — filter by city and look at what's actually posted there, not a national site that mixes old ads with active ones. Walk the neighborhood too. Talk to tea shop owners or security guards; they know which landlords are reliable and which ones are known troublemakers.

sections.heading: Always Visit in Person and Check the Physical Space
sections.body: Never book a PG from photos alone. Visit during the day and again in the evening if possible — you need to see natural light, ventilation, water pressure, and how quiet (or loud) the area actually is. Open the cupboards, check the bathroom plumbing, test the WiFi speed yourself, and look at the common areas. Ask to see where the kitchen is, how clean it is, and whether residents actually cook or if it's a 'no cooking allowed' setup. Count the windows in your room — a single window room in a hot city is miserable. Check if there's backup water (overhead tank or borewell) or if it's just municipal supply. If the landlord or manager refuses to let you see certain rooms or areas, that's a red flag — walk away.

sections.heading: Talk to Current Residents, Not Just the Landlord
sections.body: Ask if you can speak to one or two current residents for 5 minutes. A good landlord won't mind. Ask them: How long have you lived here? Any surprise charges or rules added after you moved in? How often is there water shortage? Is the landlord responsive when something breaks? Do neighbors cause issues? If current residents seem happy and have been there 6+ months, that's a strong signal. If they seem evasive, stressed, or say they're leaving soon, ask why. Pay attention to maintenance — if the building looks worn but the bathrooms are clean and the water system works, the landlord cares enough. If it looks neglected, move on.

sections.heading: Get Everything in Writing Before You Move In
sections.body: This is non-negotiable. A verbal agreement means nothing when a landlord suddenly changes the rent or locks you out. Insist on a written agreement that includes: rent amount, what's included (WiFi, water, electricity, furniture), deposit amount, notice period for both you and the landlord, what happens if something breaks, house rules (guest policy, noise hours, kitchen use), and the landlord's full name and phone number. Make sure the agreement mentions the exact move-in date and lease duration. If the landlord says "it's just a simple arrangement, no need for papers," that's a massive red flag — they're avoiding a paper trail for a reason. Take a photo of the agreement with both signatures. Keep a copy.

sections.heading: Verify the Landlord's Ownership and Check for Hidden Costs
sections.body: Ask to see proof of ownership or at least an electricity bill or property tax receipt in the landlord's name. If they can't provide it, they might be a middleman or an unauthorized tenant subleasing — and you could be evicted if the real owner finds out. Ask explicitly about all costs upfront: Is there a maintenance fee? A water/electricity surcharge? A WiFi charge? Do I pay for garbage collection? What happens if I need WiFi repair — who pays? Some landlords quote rent but then add 20% in "hidden" charges later. Write down the total monthly cost and get it in the agreement. Ask about the deposit too — what exactly needs to happen for you to get it back fully? No deductions for normal wear and tear should be allowed.

sections.heading: Use SafetyFirst Checks Before Handing Over Money
sections.body: Before you pay a deposit, do a final safety sweep. Is there proper ventilation and natural light in your room? Check the electrical outlets — are they grounded, or do they look dodgy? Does the bathroom have a geyser and does it work? Is there fire safety equipment (extinguisher, emergency exit)? Ask about Internet speed — get the landlord to run a speed test right in front of you on their own WiFi. If the speed is much lower than promised, it's a sign of overselling to other tenants. For women renters: Is there a safe common area? Is the building well-lit at night? Are there female residents already living there (which usually means the landlord manages women's safety seriously)? Pay the deposit via bank transfer, never cash — you'll have a record. Ask for a deposit receipt. Delay handing over the full amount until you've moved in and confirmed everything works.

faqs.question: What's a fair PG deposit in Bangalore?
faqs.answer: Typically one month's rent, sometimes two for longer agreements. Get it in writing along with the exact conditions for refund (usually when you move out, after inspecting for damage). Landlords sometimes try to deduct for minor scratches — push back on this.

faqs.question: How do I know if a PG is safe?
faqs.answer: Visit at different times of day, check the neighborhood vibe, ask current residents, and look at the building's security (gate, lighting, emergency contacts posted). Trust your gut — if it feels sketchy, it probably is. Safe PGs usually have engaged landlords and stable, long-term residents.

faqs.question: Should I use a broker or find PGs directly?
faqs.answer: Direct is better if you can manage it — you avoid broker fees and have a direct line to the landlord. Use platforms like LocalsIndia to find direct owner listings. If you use a broker, confirm they're registered and ask for their commission structure in writing.

faqs.question: What if the landlord asks for cash-only payment?
faqs.answer: Be cautious. Cash-only usually means they're avoiding tax records or are unlicensed. Insist on a bank transfer or post-dated checks so you have proof of payment. If they refuse, find another PG.

faqs.question: Can I negotiate rent or deposit in Bangalore PGs?
faqs.answer: In many cases, yes — especially if you commit for longer (6–12 months) or if the area has high vacancy. Try negotiating a discount for advance payment or a shorter notice period requirement. Worst they can say is no.

faqs.question: What red flags should make me walk away immediately?
faqs.answer: Landlord refuses to let you see the room, demands cash-only, won't provide a written agreement, current residents seem unhappy or evasive, or the place looks filthy and unmaintained. Also walk away if the rent seems too good to be true — it usually is.
